lessons.title: Defining & Calling Function Declarations
lessons.description: Learn how to create reusable blocks of code using function declarations — the most basic building block of organized JavaScript.

sections.heading: What is a function?
paragraphs: A function is a named block of code that you can run whenever you want. Instead of writing the same logic multiple times, you write it once inside a function and call it by name whenever you need it. Functions are the foundation of reusable, organized code.

sections.heading: Declaring a function
paragraphs: To create a function, use the function keyword followed by a name, parentheses, and curly braces. The code inside the braces only runs when you call the function.
list: function — the keyword that starts the declaration
{} — curly braces contain the function's code

sections.heading: Calling a function
paragraphs: To run a function, write its name followed by parentheses: sayHello(). This is called calling or invoking the function. The code inside executes, and then the program continues after the call.

codeExamples.heading: Your first function
explanation: The function sayHello is defined once but called twice.
Each call runs both console.log lines inside the function.
Notice the function is defined before it is called — this matters for function declarations.

codeExamples.heading: Functions that do different things
explanation: Each function has its own code block that runs independently.
calculateArea declares its own variables inside — they only exist while the function runs.
Functions can do anything: calculate values, print messages, or perform complex tasks.

practice.task: Create a function called printDate that logs today's date to the console using new Date(). Call it three times.
hints: Close with } and then call printDate(); three times.
practice.note: Try adding a second function that prints a different message, then alternate calling both.

keyTakeaways: A function is a reusable block of code defined with function name() { }.
Defining a function does not run it — you must call it with name().
Functions can be called as many times as you want, and each call runs the code inside independently.
lessons.challenge: Write a function logUserInfo that declares a name variable and an age variable inside it, then logs a message like "Name: Alex, Age: 25". Call it with different values by changing the variables inside the function.

lessons.title: Function Expressions vs Declarations
lessons.description: Understand the two ways to create functions in JavaScript — declarations and expressions — and when each one is appropriate.

sections.heading: Two ways to make a function
paragraphs: JavaScript gives you two syntaxes for creating functions: declarations and expressions. Both produce the same kind of function, but they behave differently in one important way — hoisting.

sections.heading: Function declarations
paragraphs: A function declaration starts with function followed by a name. Declarations are hoisted, meaning you can call the function before the line where it is defined. JavaScript moves declarations to the top of their scope behind the scenes.
list: Starts with function keyword and a name
Hoisted — can be called before the definition line

sections.heading: Function expressions
paragraphs: A function expression assigns an anonymous (or named) function to a variable. They are not hoisted — you must define them before you call them. Function expressions are often used for short, one-time callbacks.
list: Stored in a variable like const fn = function() { }
Not hoisted — must be defined before use
Common for callbacks and short, throwaway functions

codeExamples.heading: Declaration vs expression — hoisting difference
explanation: greet() works before its definition because declarations are hoisted.
farewell() throws an error because the variable exists but has not been assigned yet.
With const, the variable is in the temporal dead zone until the assignment line.

codeExamples.heading: When to use each one
explanation: double is a declaration — it is named, reusable, and can be called anywhere in its scope.
The anonymous function inside .map() is an expression — it is short, unnamed, and used once.
In modern code, arrow functions (covered in topic 2.2) are usually preferred for expressions.

practice.task: Create a function declaration called add that logs a + b. Then create a function expression called multiply that does the same with *. Call both.
hints: Expression: const multiply = function(a, b) { console.log(a * b); };
practice.note: Try calling the function expression before you define it — what error do you get?

keyTakeaways: Function declarations (function name() { }) are hoisted — you can call them before the definition line.
Function expressions (const name = function() { }) are not hoisted — define them before calling.
Use declarations for named, reusable functions; use expressions for short callbacks.
lessons.challenge: Write a function declaration that logs "I am hoisted" and call it before the definition. Then write a function expression and try to call it before defining it. Compare the two results.

lessons.title: Passing Arguments & Setting Default Parameters
lessons.description: Make functions flexible by accepting input values — and set sensible defaults so callers can skip optional arguments.

sections.heading: Parameters vs arguments
paragraphs: A parameter is a variable listed in the function definition: function greet(name). An argument is the actual value you pass when calling: greet("Alex"). The parameter name receives the argument "Alex" inside the function.

sections.heading: Multiple parameters
paragraphs: Separate parameters with commas. The order matters — the first argument goes to the first parameter, the second to the second, and so on. If you pass fewer arguments than parameters, the missing ones become undefined.

sections.heading: Default parameters
paragraphs: You can give parameters default values using =. If the caller does not provide that argument, the default is used. This makes functions easier to call and prevents undefined bugs.
list: function greet(name = "Guest") — defaults to "Guest" if no argument is passed
Defaults apply when the argument is undefined (not when it is null or 0)
Defaults work from left to right — you can skip trailing parameters

codeExamples.heading: Parameters and arguments in action
explanation: The first argument "Alex" goes to the first parameter name.
When timeOfDay is not provided, it becomes undefined.
This is why default parameters are useful — they fill in missing values automatically.

codeExamples.heading: Default parameters prevent undefined
explanation: When "Sam" is passed, only name gets a value — timeOfDay uses its default.
With no arguments, both parameters use their defaults.
undefined as an argument also triggers the default — useful for skipping middle parameters.

practice.task: Write a function calculateTotal(price, taxRate = 0.1) that logs the total price including tax. Test with different values: calculateTotal(100), calculateTotal(50, 0.2), and calculateTotal(200, 0.05).
hints: Inside the function, calculate: let total = price + price * taxRate;
The default taxRate = 0.1 means 10% tax when no second argument is passed.
practice.note: What happens if you call calculateTotal("100")? JavaScript will try to add a string and a number.

keyTakeaways: Parameters are in the definition; arguments are what you pass when calling.
If you pass fewer arguments than parameters, the missing ones are undefined.
Default parameters (param = value) fill in missing arguments automatically.
Default values trigger when the argument is undefined or not provided at all.
lessons.challenge: Write a function createUser(name, role = "user", isActive = true) that logs an object with all three properties. Call it three ways: with all arguments, with just a name, and with name and role.

lessons.title: Rest Parameters (...args) for Variable Arguments
lessons.description: Write functions that accept any number of arguments using the rest parameter syntax — perfect for flexible, future-proof functions.

sections.heading: Why rest parameters?
paragraphs: Sometimes you do not know how many arguments a function will receive. A function that adds two numbers is easy — but what about one that adds five, or ten, or a hundred? Rest parameters let you collect any number of arguments into a single array.

sections.heading: The syntax
paragraphs: Put ... before the last parameter name. That parameter becomes an array containing all remaining arguments. It must be the last parameter — you cannot have anything after it.
list: function sum(...numbers) — numbers is an array of all arguments
function log(first, ...rest) — first gets the first argument, rest gets the rest as an array
The rest parameter must be the last parameter in the list

sections.heading: Rest vs arguments object
paragraphs: JavaScript also has an old arguments object inside every function. Rest parameters are better: they give you a real array (with .map(), .filter(), etc.), they work with arrow functions, and their intent is clearer. Always prefer rest parameters over arguments.

codeExamples.heading: Sum any number of values
explanation: ...numbers collects all arguments into an array — sum(1, 2, 3) gives numbers = [1, 2, 3].
The for...of loop iterates over every number in the array.
With no arguments, numbers is an empty array, so the sum is 0.

codeExamples.heading: Combining named and rest parameters
explanation: prefix captures the first argument — it is a regular named parameter.
...messages captures all remaining arguments as an array.
This pattern is common in logging utilities — a category label plus any number of messages.

practice.task: Write a function findMax(...nums) that returns the largest number from any number of arguments. Test with findMax(3, 7, 2, 9, 1) and findMax(42).
hints: Use Math.max(...nums) to find the maximum — the spread operator passes the array as individual arguments.
Alternatively, loop through nums and track the largest value manually.
practice.note: Try passing strings like findMax("3", "7", "2") — what does Math.max return?

keyTakeaways: Rest parameters (...param) collect any number of arguments into a real array.
They must be the last parameter in the function definition.
Rest parameters are preferred over the old arguments object — they work with arrays and arrow functions.
Use rest parameters when a function needs to handle a variable number of inputs.
lessons.challenge: Write a function concatenate(separator, ...words) that joins all the word arguments using the separator. Example: concatenate(" - ", "hello", "world", "js") should return "hello - world - js".

lessons.title: Returning Values with return (vs Implicit undefined)
lessons.description: Make functions produce results you can use — and understand what happens when a function has no return statement.

sections.heading: Why return values?
paragraphs: A function that only logs to the console is limited. To reuse a calculation or transformation, the function must send the result back to wherever it was called. The return keyword does this — it stops the function and gives back a value.

sections.heading: How return works
paragraphs: When JavaScript hits a return statement, it immediately exits the function and produces the given value. Any code after return is never reached. If return is used without a value (or not used at all), the function returns undefined.

sections.heading: Implicit undefined
paragraphs: Every function that does not explicitly return a value gives back undefined. This is not an error — it just means the function was written for its side effects (like logging or modifying the DOM) rather than producing a result. Knowing when to return and when to just execute is a key skill.

codeExamples.heading: Returning a calculated value
explanation: return a + b; sends the result back to wherever the function was called.
The returned value can be stored in a variable or used directly in expressions.
The first return in checkAge exits early — the second return is never reached when age is negative.

codeExamples.heading: Functions without return return undefined
explanation: sayHello() prints "Hello!" but returns undefined because there is no return.
multiply calculates the product but never returns it — the result is lost.
This is a common beginner mistake. If a function should produce a result, always use return.

practice.task: Write a function isEven(number) that returns true if the number is even, false otherwise. Store the result in a variable and log it. Then write a function doubleAll(arr) that returns a new array with every number doubled.
hints: For doubleAll: create an empty array, loop through the input, push doubled values, and return the new array.
Remember: if you forget the return, the function gives back undefined.

keyTakeaways: return sends a value back from the function and immediately exits it.
Functions without a return statement return undefined implicitly.
Always use return when a function should produce a result — not just log it.
Code after return is unreachable and will never execute.
lessons.challenge: Write a function calculateAverage(...numbers) that uses rest parameters to accept any number of values and returns their average. Test with calculateAverage(10, 20, 30) — it should return 20.
